title: 237. can gen z actually make change? let’s talk burnout, hope, + leadership feat. amanda litman
description_html: how gen z can lead with hope (even when it feels impossible)? today’s guest is amanda litman— the co-founder and president of run for something, a nonprofit organization that recruits and supports young leaders to run for state and local office. she has written two books geared toward the next generation of political leaders, was named one of the time next 100, and is currently a 2025-2026 obama foundation usa leader.

summary: sadie talks with amanda litman, co-founder of run for something, about how gen z can lead with hope even when politics feels hopeless. they discuss getting involved locally, the disconnect between gen z's political engagement and burnout, and how young leaders are changing workplace culture. amanda shares why the four day work week works, what might be possible if things didn't suck, and how to practice leadership skills before you're officially in charge. practical and grounding for anyone trying to make change without losing themselves.

paragraphs.text: Welcome to She Persisted, the Gen Z mental health podcast. I'm your host, Sadie Sutton. Let's get into it. To get stronger, to get to the other side of change, you have to go through a little bit of pain. It's part of the process. You gotta burn it down a little bit to build it back up. That's gonna make it really hard. Like you don't wanna do it. That trap of, ugh, like it's so much easier just to stick with the way we've been doing things. Like it's tradition, it's how we've always done it. It's the only way I know. That can keep you from imagining a better future.

It is no coincidence that I am releasing this interview right before election month, given how incredibly turbulent the current political landscape is and how Gen Z is starting to shift from school to a lot of uncertainty around career opportunities and adulthood. I think this episode is coming at the perfect time. So hello, hello, and welcome back to She Persisted. Today's episode is going to serve as pretty much your guide to navigating the current world and job market as a member of Gen Z who is looking to inspire change and clean up many of the messes that we're dealing with as a society.

And we have the perfect guest to speak on this topic. We have Amanda Littman, the co-founder and president of Run for Something, a nonprofit organization that recruits and supports young leaders to run for state and local offices. She's also worked with Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton campaigns, and has been named one of Time's list of the next 100 who are shaping the future and defining the next generation of leadership.

So it's safe to say she is incredibly qualified to share insights and advice for anyone in Gen Z who is looking to make an actual impact on today's world but don't know where to start. So if this sounds like you, this episode will leave you feeling empowered and inspired to take on the workforce or the current political landscape and make meaningful change. So without further ado, let's dive in.

Well, thank you so much for joining me today, Amanda. I'm so excited to have you on the show. We are recording this at a very interesting time. I've been hosting the podcast for five years now, and I think this is a conversation that is top of mind for a lot of people, or at least has become top of mind. So I'm really excited to get your expert insights and thoughts for people that

want to lean more into creating change, potentially going down the political path, or just being better leaders in their own communities and with the people that they come into contact with on a daily basis. So thank you for joining me. My pleasure, Sadie. Thanks for having me. Of course. So to get started, can you give us a bit of a background? You have had such a fascinating career and gone in so many different directions, been so involved in so many incredible campaigns.

And so I'm really curious how you landed in this space and started working on creating really meaningful change and really powerful change and making really big shifts in how our society functions and operates and thinks, which is relevant to so many areas, especially mental health. Because I think we forget that policy is such a huge part of that and who's advocating on our behalf can be like life or death.

So I'm really excited to get your thoughts on how people can feel more empowered and have more of a sense of agency because that's such a big part of thriving as a society. Yeah. So I'll stop by telling you a little bit about myself and then we can get into it. So I was born and raised in Northern Virginia. I went to Northwestern for college where I studied American studies with a focus on gender and politics. My senior year of school, I got an internship on the Obama reelect doing online fundraising and volunteer recruitment.

I was hired before I graduated, worked for the president's campaign, which we won. So fun. Stayed in Chicago to work for the president's nonprofit for about a year. Moved to Florida in 2014 to work for the governor's race. And then moved to New York in 2015 to work for Secretary Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign. I was her email director. So again, online fundraising, volunteer recruitment, that kind of thing. We lost. That was sad.

Yes. About a week. I remember watching that CNN live updates and it was a wild, wild night. Zero stars. Don't recommend. So I, about a week after election day in 2016, I started hearing from friends I'd gone to high school and college with. Hey, Amanda, I'm a public school teacher in Chicago. I'm thinking about running for office. You're the only person I know that works in politics. What do I do? And at the time, if you were young, I was in my mid-20s, and you wanted to do more than vote and more than volunteer, there was no way you could go that would answer your call. And that, to me, felt like really big symptoms, both in our democracy and in the Democratic Party. So I reached out to a whole bunch of people with an idea. What if we started an organization that would be a big part of the party?

kind of like Emily's List, which helps pro-choice Democratic women run for office, but to help people like my friend from college who wants to run for the first time. One of those folks became my co-founder, Ross Morales-Riquetto. We wrote a plan, we built a website, and then we launched Run for Something on Trump's first inauguration day, thinking it'd be really small. We maybe would get 100 people who want to run in the first year. In the first week, we had 1,000 people sign up.

As of today, we're up to more than 220,000 young people all across the country who've raised their hands to say they want to run. We've helped elect more than 1,500 across 49 states, mostly women and people of color, all under the age of 40 at the first election. And I also wrote two books in the process. So that's me.

Okay, I have so many areas that I want to go there and so many things to touch on. I think the first is the beginning of your story where you were able to get involved in such a hands-on way in college and in undergrad. And I'm really curious... what that process looks like. Because I think a lot of us, we can vote for the first time in college. College campuses are a very political place. I was at Penn and it kind of felt like there was a foot in each camp and everyone was talking about all the things given the history of the school. And even with that feeling like my vote had a lot of power and I was voting in a swing state,

getting involved beyond that even though like the rally was being held in Philadelphia and you were seeing all these things on the news as far as meaningful steps you could take it still did feel somewhat out of reach beyond like phone banking and getting your family and friends to go out and swing states rather than home states, depending on where they're from. So can you talk to us about how you can get involved and support politicians that are aligned with your beliefs or individuals in your community when you don't have that career experience or you're not years into working in politics? Mm-hmm.

The best thing you can do is go hyperlocal. I think this is true, especially when you're a student, because the people that govern city councils and state legislatures in these college towns can have a big impact on whether you can afford to stay in your college town if you want to. Like how easy or hard it is to find an apartment off campus or a house off campus. Yeah. They really do affect how expensive your tuition is. It's often set on the state legislative level by the state government.

There is so much work that these local offices do that affect your life as a student. But on the other side of it, they're also so much fun. Like if you are a student or a recent grad and you want to get involved locally, you can very quickly become the campaign manager or the volunteer director or the communications director for these local races because not that many people do it.

So you can very quickly become a big fish in a small pond. And your experience as a student, as a member of the community is so invaluable to these campaigns. They're also just a great way to get to know the candidates themselves. And a good reminder that politicians are people, and people are flawed, but that you can really get exposure to it firsthand. Yeah.

Yeah. So I have a lot of things that I want to pick your brain on because you are so tapped into this space. And it feels like we have quite the like dialectic of, like you said, Gen Z is so involved. You have so many people raising their hands saying like, we want to help, we want to get involved, we don't just care, but we'd like to take action and advocate on behalf of others and create change. And I also feel like there's this paralyzing sense of hopelessness and like a disconnect from what's happening on a larger level.

and what you see in your day-to-day or how you see things and how others see things. And we're seeing this gender gap emerge. And there's huge shifts in how our demographic of where we're at age-wise compares to other ages historically. And so I'm really curious what you're seeing with Gen Z and why we might have this like, some people are so on board to take action and feeling hopeful and ready to go. And others are like, how did we get here? I don't know what's going on. And I don't know how to move forward.

And I think part of it is that we got to this point because people felt disillusioned. And I think that the only way out of it is deep organizing and deep work. It doesn't mean just electoral. Like, I think elections are a key part of it, but not the only part of it. And I think there's often pushback. I know I get it where I'm like, you have to vote in local elections. Well, electoralism doesn't solve any problems. Yeah.

Well, it doesn't solve all our problems, but it's kind of like if you wanted to make an apple pie, but you didn't have any apples. You need it. You just it's an important, necessary ingredient. It's not the only ingredient you need, but it's a necessary ingredient. And I think a thing that we have often forgotten, I say we broad scale, anyone who's like not a fascist or a Nazi at this point, is that winning the presidency, much like electoralism, is a necessary but alone not sufficient part of the process.

Yeah. You know, we have to also win city councils and school boards and state legislatures and library boards and water districts and community college boards and everything else. Or we're missing the fundamental way in which power gets held in this country. We don't have one one massive government. We have the federal government and then 50 state governments and thousands of county governments and thousands more city governments and districts within those. And those build on each other. And if we aren't careful, we're.

The bad people take over the little ones and then they make it much, much harder for us to win the big ones. Yeah. I like how you mentioned how many layers and checks and balances truly exist in the system. And I think a lot of people listening, if they're following political updates, there are so many moments of fear and anxiety and that hopelessness of what is happening. And I think...

Most of the people listening are Gen Z women, and I think that is one group especially who is really impacted by the current political landscape. And so I'm curious from your perspective, having so many young individuals wanting to get involved and running for office, but I'm curious what your thoughts are there. Like, is it truly a position where you're seeing these things and you're like, yes, this has a direct impact? Or when you're reading these headlines, is it more kind of what you just said where you're like, okay, but we have all these layers and...

And all hope is not lost. And there is a disconnect between like my day to day life and this one thing that was said on Twitter. Like what is your thought process there for people who are really struggling with that in a big way? Well, I think it's really important to remember that there are a lot of things that the president can do that can hurt people. I don't want to ever undersell that.

And there's a lot of things we can do locally to protect people and to advance progress, especially on the things that directly affect your quality of life. Like the cost of housing, cost of child care, your access to reproductive health, your access to gender-affirmative care, school lunches, library funding, how... Easy or hard it is to open a business. That stuff is shaped on the local level, which means you can have a lot of say there. And I think that grounding fact is what keeps me hopeful, which you need to be. You need to be hopeful. Otherwise, it's impossible to get out of bed in the morning.

Yes. No, I completely agree. And I definitely share that point of view. And I even go on the days where it's like, okay, I'm feeling less hopeful. It's like, but what is going to get us moving forward and get things to shift and change? And it's some amount of hope that then inspires action. That's right. And so trying to then get to that mindset so that things actually...

will change and be different rather than just being like stuck in this. OK, here's the cards we've been dealt and we do nothing at this point and we're just on this road. So we keep driving. And so you have so many people as a part of Run for Something that are working to make this change and that really want to have a very active role there. I'm curious your thoughts on the future of politics as Gen Z gets more involved.

getting to know these people, supporting them in this process, in this early stage of their journey, what do you think is going to shift and change over the coming years and how we're describing the issues that we're struggling with on a day-to-day, how we're reaching people, what people care about, what is inspiring action, all of those things as we see this like new era of politics unfold.

And I think Gen Z brings a really different attitude to politics in a good way. I think that's true both in politics and outside of it. And I wrote this book called When We're in Charge. It's about Gen Z and millennial leadership and the way that we do things differently. And I think that's really what we're seeing in politics, at work, in institutions, in systems, that the way we did things yesterday does not have to dictate the way we do things tomorrow. Yeah. And that mentality is really, really powerful. Mm-hmm. Really powerful.

I want to dive into your book a bit more because you mentioned that, and I would love your thoughts on those different elements of leadership. You mentioned that just because we've done things historically doesn't mean that it has to move forward this way. What are those aspects of leadership that are so different in Gen Z and millennial leaders versus what we have done historically, which we can work to change and not accept at face value?

You know, I think things like work has to suck. I don't think that's true. Yeah. I just don't. Yeah. I mean, I think work is hard and like sometimes some parts of it are not that fun, but work doesn't have to suck. If leaders don't want it to, it doesn't. The idea that you have to be messy at work or that authenticity inherently requires like messiness. Yeah.

It doesn't. And of course, vulnerability, but also involves boundaries. I think that is a really important distinction that too many people have forgotten. I think really important to think about clarity of communication, to think about norms of communication. I think right now it's very easy to say diversity is a fad. It is not. It is both a business imperative and a moral imperative. It's also going to be a lived reality for millennials and Gen Z. Yeah.

Better learn how to handle it well. Yeah. And then really thinking about how can you be effective and also compassionate? Like how can you hold getting shit done and being a good person in the same space? Yeah. Those are not competing. They're not mutually exclusive. I think too many business executives and corporate CEOs and especially some of the older leaders have sort of assumed that in order to get the best results out of people, you have to work around the clock. You have to grind it out. You have to like yell and punish and penalize. Like you don't. You just don't. I reject that. I don't. I refuse to believe that's the case. Mm hmm.

I'm curious if you were entering the workforce this year, then the coming years, I just started my first full-time role. What things you would push back on or even set your own boundaries around that kind of are more aligned with those historical ideals or those things that we've accepted as this is what work looks like. Here are the expectations that are held. Here's just how it works. And those things that you would shift on an individual level. And then later in your career, make sure that those are systemic and that your team and your community are also kind of following in those footsteps.

You know, I think a lot of it has to come with from the leadership of setting the right tone of modeling the kind of behavior you want to see. But I think it is always appropriate for especially, you know, first time employees to like really demand clarity about what success looks like. Yeah. You know, if somebody asks you to do something, it is not rude or is not pushing the limit to respectfully and politely but clearly ask, can you tell me what it looks like when this is done well?

Yeah. Can you tell me what this looks like when this is done poorly? Can you explain to me why the timeline is and why that looks good? I want to learn. sometimes the executive or the leadership hasn't quite thought through that and they might not be able to answer it. And then it's on them because asking for success metrics is not a bad thing. Yeah. I also think being really clear about capacity, you know, I know is very trendy to like, I'm not going to answer email after five o'clock. I'm not going to, I'm going to log off. Like definitely do that.

And if you are having an issue where your work is requiring you to or being asked to, like, again, hey, this seems like a place that wants people to be able to do this work sustainably. I cannot currently commit to complete my workload and also do that. Can you help me reprioritize? Yeah. Like, this is a skill around managing up that is really hard. But when you do it right, it will make your whole life better and will also get you what you want without being an asshole to your boss. Mm-hmm.

The final thing I would say, especially if you're early in your career, do not treat the internet like your group chat. Man, do people forget that the internet is forever and that if you are going to shit talk your employers or your bosses or your colleagues online, assume they are going to see it. Do not post anything you don't want your boss to get in the form of a New York Times homepage news alert. You know, that's what we used to say in politics. Like don't put anything in writing that you wouldn't want to see on the front page of the New York Times.

treat everything like that yeah i know that can be really hard because it's like this is how we live this is how we communicate i want to be myself i was like you can be yourself in your group chat you don't have to be yourself on instagram maybe your small group chat maybe not like the one with 45 people on snapchat that you guys are all like updating on maybe like your your close friends yeah like you can keep it on close ease it's fine

Yeah, I am curious if there are examples of those or things that like there's that generational divide where bosses are like, how on earth could someone say that? And Gen Z is like, wait, that's wrong. Like, what are you talking about? That is totally fine. Are there any examples of those that people should really be aware of that they're not already flagging as like, this is something I should be staying away from and I'm creating challenges for myself down the road?

You know, I think a lot about mental health. I know this is like a topic for you as well. Like, I think it's really important. Like, as a boss, I have a therapist. I see my therapist every two weeks. It's on my calendar, blocked out in the middle of the day. And it says so quite boldly, like, 11 a.m. therapy. Yeah. I think it's really important both that I do that for myself, for my partner, for my kids, my parents.

my mental health and to model for my team that I want them to take the time to do that. Yeah. But it's encouraged. It is not sick leave. It's not PTO. You don't need to make it work outside of your work day. Like it's just part of being good at your job is taking care of yourself. And you don't need to tell my employees what I talk about in therapy. Yeah.

You're like, here's the TLDR from therapy. Here are the updates going into action. Like, no, like that's between me and my mental health. Like for professional. I think reminding yourself that that is like a boundary that you can set. That distinction of I go to therapy. Here's all the things I talk about my therapist. Yeah. One is appropriate and one is not. And being really distinct about those limits.

Yeah. I think it's also worth kind of having that distinction, like you mentioned, of like what you've normalized and what you wouldn't pass judgment on and what others might, even if it's not right to pass judgment or right to think about you differently as a result of that information. And I think mental health is one of those areas that's still a challenge.

Like being vulnerable is very good. It's very important. It helps like alleviate distress. You feel more validated and connected. Like it's great to talk about your mental health challenges. However, in certain contexts, it might not be the most effective. You have to be aware of your audience. And regardless of if it's right, if your boss would treat you differently or if your co-worker might then tiptoe around and like not remind you about things because you don't want to get stressed, even though like you might need that reminder. And then it comes and like bites you in the ass down the road.

I think it's very important to be mindful of that audience and aware of where people's mentalities might be at, which might be very different from yours. And just like understanding that your problems, especially when you're in a leadership role, my problems, if I don't hold like a really strong boundary, can become everyone's problems. I don't want that to be the case. Yeah. Yeah. I don't.

A hundred percent. I think that's one of the like and we'll talk about in a minute tips for Gen Z who are already leaders because you depending on the field you go into you like very quickly start helping others and supporting them. You're a point person for something. I'm going into like academia and research is the plan at this point. So you're already working to support other undergrads and help train people.

And it's like, okay, I was just an undergrad last year. And so like you do have some responsibility and it's important to know those skills. But yeah, no, I completely agree with what you mentioned there. Before we move into those leadership skills, one thing you talk about in the book, which is a hot topic is the four-day work week. Can you tell me a little bit more about that? Because most people have probably heard about this concept at some point. And like you mentioned, it's a very real possibility for us to see pan out in a wide,

scale way. I love the four-day work week. I think everyone should consider it. And there's just a study, a new study out by the four-day work week global program that showed once again, as we have seen, asking people to work four days a week for the same pay without cutting their pay, increased mental health, increased physical health, no change to productivity. And in fact, in about a third of survey respondents, increased productivity. Mm-hmm.

Run for Something, the organization I run, has had a four-day work week since 2022. It is transformative. We saw when we did the pilot program that every stat you'd want to see go up around staff engagement, retention, job life satisfaction, enjoyment went up. Every stat you'd want to see go down around exhaustion, anxiety, depression went down. And it has been incredible for keeping people and for basically every time we have an open role, hundreds if not thousands of resumes come in.

And I will say, like, I know maybe your listeners aren't quite there yet, but as a parent, it has been magical. Because I get to do four days of work with my job. On my Fridays, my daughters go to daycare. Because sometimes I have stuff to do and like, yeah, whatever. Yeah. Errands take up a lot of time. It's horrible. Being an adult is hard. Being an adult is hard. So I have Fridays to myself, which means I make doctor's appointments. I go to a yoga class. I get my nails done. I have lunch with a friend. And then I get to go into a weekend with my tiny kids. I have a two and a half year old and a baby.

And I'm refreshed. I'm ready to tackle the 48 hours of intensive parenting. It is the only way that I've been able to survive the last couple of years and do this work in a way that allows me to keep doing it for a long time. Yeah. And I think going back to what we kind of touched on at the beginning of the conversation, which is ways that you can get involved in your local community or ways that you can work to make change. A lot of the times, those don't perfectly fit into your job description. And so being able to have the bandwidth and the capacity.

to engage in those other elements. Like we're having this interview after I finished up the work day and I was able to get off early because my boss is super flexible with hours and when we have other things, that's really great to be able to make positive change and continue working on those goals and feel like you're making a difference while balancing.

that work routine and making progress there because five days, nine to five, plus all these extra hours working on these very real projects or initiatives or campaigns, it does add up and it's challenging to not burn out with all of those responsibilities on your plate. I mean, this is the overarching question of basically all the work I do, which is what might be possible if things didn't suck? Yeah. Like, what might be possible if our political leadership didn't suck? What might be possible if work didn't leave you drained at the end of the day? Like, what could it open up for you as a person, as a partner, as a parent, as a friend, as a citizen? Yeah. Like, what kind of time could you have? What kind of energy could you have? What kind of art could you create? It is really exciting to imagine that a better way actually is possible. Yeah.

Yeah, and it invokes a lot of hope, like we talked about. Like it can be challenging to fall into these other mindsets, but that question gives so much hope for what could come next. And I'm curious for people listening who hopefully will step into these roles and create change either on their teams and their communities on a larger scale. What are those things that suck that you hope to chip away at and see shift over the next 20, 30, 40 years?

I hope we can build a ton more housing and make housing costs go down. I hope that it can become part of the American dream that people can buy homes again if they want to. I hope we can get universal child care. I hope we can get paid family leave. I also think more, you know, close to home, I guess. I think it is possible for us to have bosses, company founders, and executives who see people as full people first and worker bees second. Who create workplaces that are inclusive and welcoming and compassionate. Who pay people enough that they can, you know, get the mental health care they need and the physical health care they need. And live a life outside of work and have flexible schedules such that they have time to do those things.

Yeah. And that maybe if we do so, people will have more energy and time to be in community with each other. Because think about how many times you're like, ma'am, I would love to go out to dinner with a friend, but I've had a long time. I'm tired. Yeah. Like, what if you weren't tired? What if we weren't tired? Yes. I love that question in way of thinking about things because especially as things with college ramped up and work, like I give myself a lot of grace with when I am tired and being like, you know what, I'm going to read my book and get it.

get things cleaned up and I'm not going to go out to dinner or do all these crazy activities and that's okay. And it's great because it prevents burnout. But reframing that of like, okay, what if the context that I was in didn't make me feel tired or overwhelmed or burnt out? And it's not, again, it's not on the person. It's not like, what if you weren't tired from doing the same thing? But what if the context was different? And as a result of that, you were...

feeling better, had more capacity to engage with friends or family or activities that you don't have the time to do at this point. That's exactly right. So I love that. It's like, what if we change the supply instead of the demand, you know? Yes. I'm curious how hard you think it will be to shift that supply. Yeah.

Like, is this something where it's like, okay, as people that are listening to these conversations, engaging in these conversations, start having more power, they can make those shifts? Or is this something that like centuries from now, we're like, come on, guys, like we got to keep working on the work-life balance. I think it is possible because I think so much of it stems from leadership. And I think as new people take over, you know, in 2030, the youngest boomer is going to hit retirement age. Millennials and Gen Z are going to be a majority of the workforce by then. We actually get to decide if we want to keep doing things the way they've been done.

And like part of the reason I wrote the book is because there wasn't a playbook for if you knew you wanted to do it differently. Like what does that mean? What does that look like? How do you actually execute on that? There wasn't a guide to. So I wrote it. And I hope that people read it or see other people doing it differently and decide, oh, yeah, actually I can decide that I don't want to run a hundred hour a week startup. Yeah. I don't think I need to. Yeah. Mm-hmm.

I am curious, are there any thinking traps or pitfalls that might happen when the demographic of the workforce shifts? that would cause us to kind of continue this norm rather than work to change it. You know, I think part of it is just the status quo is easy. Yeah. Like change is hard. I mean, you think about, I don't know if you are like a fitness person. I'm not currently at this stage in my life, but- Love a good walk. Love a good walk, love a good yoga class. But you know the theory here, which is that in order to get stronger, you have to destroy a little bit. Like you lift weights enough so that you destroy the muscle fibers and then they rebuild a little bit better.
